paper_title: FilmFlow: Agentic System for 3D Virtual Film Cinematography

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Complex camera motion is central to visual storytelling, yet translating cinematographic intent into controllable, executable camera trajectories remains challenging. We introduce FilmFlow, an agentic framework that converts natural-language instructions or reference videos into explicit camera trajectories for dynamic 3D environments. To generate these trajectories, a Director agent constructs executable camera plans by composing high-level motions from concurrent atomic operations that jointly control translation, rotation, and framing. The Director is supported by three specialized agents: an Interpreter that extracts scene-grounded cinematographic intent, a Scout that selects initial viewpoints, and a Critic that evaluates rendered results and provides visual feedback for iterative plan refinement. We also introduce CinemaBench, comprising 150 Blender scenes from self-created and licensed sources, with five camera instructions per scene for 750 text-directed tasks and 60 reference videos associated with a subset of scenes. CinemaBench supports evaluation of both text-directed camera generation and video reference-directed camera generation. Across a diverse set of evaluated baselines, FilmFlow achieves the strongest benchmark performance and the highest user preference, demonstrating effective spatial reasoning, temporal coordination, and visual composition for executable 3D cinematography.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Camera movement is fundamental expressive device in filmmaking, shaping viewers attention, emotional engagement, and understanding of scene (Brown, 2021). gradual push-in can emphasize characters reaction, while pullback can reveal surrounding action and change the meaning of moment. Achieving these narrative effects requires carefully coordinating camera movement, framing, and subject motion throughout shot (Block, 2020). Advances in spatial intelligence open up new possibilities for automating this coordination, enabling AI systems to reason about scene geometry and spatial relationships. Yet translating this understanding into cinematographically meaningful camera behavior remains challenging. Filmmakers often communicate their intentions through natural-language descriptions or reference footage, leaving the spatial and temporal decisions needed for execution implicit. Prior work has made substantial progress toward automated cinematography, from rule-based and optimization-based camera control (Christie et al., 2008) to learned trajectory generation conditioned on textual descriptions (Jiang et al., 2024). More recently, ChatCam (Liu et al., 2024) uses language agent to interpret user requests and invoke camera-generation tools, while FilmAgent (Xu et al., 2025) coordinates broader filmmaking workflows through multi-agent collaboration. CinemaTraj (Li et al., 2026) further grounds camera planning in 3D scene graphs, sequentially composing parametric motion primitives and optimizing their parameters to reduce collisions and occlusions in static scenes. Building on these advances, we address two coupled challenges: maintaining intended framing as subjects move, and coordinating concurrent camera operations with distinct timing. For example, shot may orbit moving subject while rising, then begin push-in before the orbit ends. Such intent requires explicit control over how operations overlap and jointly determine camera behavior. The rendered result must also be assessed for composition and pacing, which geometric feasibility alone cannot ensure. To address these challenges, we introduce FilmFlow, an agentic framework that generates executable camera trajectories in dynamic 3D scenes from natural-language instructions or reference videos. To generate these trajectories, Director agent constructs structured camera plans by composing highlevel motions from concurrent atomic operations. Three specialized agents support the Director: an Interpreter extracts scene-grounded cinematographic intent from the input, Scout selects initial viewpoints, and Critic evaluates executed plans and their rendered results. Because poor opening constrains every later operation, the Scout searches for this viewpoint before planning; and to reuse compositions that have already succeeded, an in-context learning mechanism (Brown et al., 2020) retrieves validated demonstrations to guide the Director. We also introduce CinemaBench, comprising 150 Blender scenes from self-created and licensed sources, with five camera instructions per scene for 750 text-directed tasks and 60 reference videos associated with subset of scenes. CinemaBench supports evaluation of both text-directed camera generation and video reference-directed camera generation. Across the evaluated baselines, FilmFlow achieves the strongest benchmark performance and the highest user preference. Our contributions are threefold: Agentic cinematography in dynamic scenes. To our knowledge, FilmFlow is the first agentic framework to unify text-directed and video reference-directed camera generation in dynamic 3D scenes. The framework centers on Director that constructs executable camera plans, assisted by specialized Interpreter, Scout, and Critic agents for scene-grounded intent extraction, initial viewpoint selection, and evaluation and refinement. Concurrent motion representation and optimization. We introduce structured cameraplan representation that composes high-level motions from concurrent atomic operations, with explicit parameters and temporal intervals to coordinate translation, rotation, and framing. Critic-guided refinement loop revises individual operations, their parameters, and their timing using execution and visual feedback, while an in-context learning mechanism guides camera planning. CinemaBench. We introduce CinemaBench, comprising 150 Blender scenes, 750 textdirected tasks, and 60 reference videos associated with subset of scenes, to evaluate both text-directed and video reference-directed camera generation. FilmFlow achieves the best performance across all reported automatic metrics and the highest overall preference in user studies for both text-directed and video reference-directed camera generation among the evaluated baselines.

sections.title: 3.1 CONCURRENT ATOMIC CAMERA OPERATIONS
sections.content: Atomic camera operations. Complex cinematographic movements require coordinated changes in camera position, orientation, and framing. FilmFlow expresses such behavior through 22 atomic operations, summarized in Table 1. For each shot, the Director constructs an operation timeline: = {oi}N i=1, oi = (mi, θi, [ai, bi]), (5) where mi selects an operation, θi specifies its parameters and target references, and [ai, bi] defines its active interval. Overlapping intervals allow multiple operations to jointly control the camera. For example, Orbit, Dolly In, and Pedestal Up can produce movement that circles subject while approaching and ascending. This decomposition preserves the meaning of each constituent action and exposes its parameters and timing for subsequent refinement. Concurrent trajectory composition. We represent the camera state as c(t) = (p(t), R(t), (t)), where p(t) is its position, R(t) its orientation, and (t) its focal length; additional lens parameters are omitted for clarity. The executor first expands each atomic operation into an absolute camera-state sequence ˆci(t), using its parameters, incoming camera state, and operation-specific interpolation. sections.title: 4.3 USER STUDY
sections.content: We conduct blinded user studies for T2V and V2V separately, with method identities hidden and presentation order randomized. Forty-two participants were each assigned 10 T2V and 10 V2V trials, randomly sampled from the T2V and V2V test tasks. Each trial shows the text instruction (T2V) or reference video (V2V) alongside the outputs of all four methods. Participants rate each output on five-point scale for camera-behavior alignment, overall visual quality (aesthetics and technical fidelity), and motion smoothness; judge whether it realizes the specified camera behavior (pass or fail); and rank the outputs by overall preference. sections.title: 5 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We presented FilmFlow, an agentic framework that generates executable camera trajectories in dynamic 3D scenes from natural-language instructions or reference videos. By composing concurrent atomic operations and refining plans through execution and visual feedback, FilmFlow coordinates camera motion, subject tracking, and framing to realize cinematographic intent. In-context demonstrations further guide operation selection and temporal composition. We also introduced CinemaBench to evaluate camera generation under both input modalities. Experiments show that FilmFlow achieves the strongest benchmark performance and highest user preference among the evaluated baselines. Future work will investigate whether smaller models can achieve comparable performance through task-specific fine-tuning, and extend FilmFlow to jointly automate scene construction and camera planning.

sections.title: AI USE STATEMENT
sections.content: We used generative AI tools to improve the clarity and readability of the manuscript, assist with debugging code, generate synthetic datasets, and create the teaser figure. The authors reviewed the AI-assisted text, code changes, and teaser figure, and checked the generated data for consistency with the intended experimental setup. The authors take full responsibility for the final content of this work, including the figures, datasets, implementation, and reported results.

sections.title: ETHICS STATEMENT
sections.content: CinemaBench includes third-party scene assets and reference videos. Our release will preserve source attribution and respect applicable licenses and redistribution restrictions. Materials without redistribution permission will be excluded, with source links and acquisition instructions provided where possible. The user study received institutional ethics clearance. All participants provided informed consent, and their responses were anonymized to protect participant privacy.

sections.title: REPRODUCIBILITY STATEMENT
sections.content: We will publicly release the FilmFlow implementation, CinemaBench annotations, along with instructions for obtaining the required scene assets, to facilitate reproduction of our results.

sections.title: A TECHNICAL DETAILS OF THE AGENTIC SYSTEM
sections.content: A.1 AGENT ROLES AND STRUCTURED INTERFACES We illustrate the agent interfaces using running T2V example, linking each variable in the method overview to concrete prompt input, structured response, or rendered observation. Starting from the cinematographic input and scene observations extracted from S, we show the Interpreters object description and cinematographic script B; the Scouts candidate camera states c(k), rendered opening views R(S, c(k)), and selected opening c; and the Directors initial and revised plans (j) and (j+1). The Critic examples include both opening-view and motion evaluation, showing the evidence used to obtain scores qview and qmotion and feedback Fview and Fmotion. supplementary note below summarizes the reference-specific inputs and evaluation used for V2V. The T2V example requests dolly zoom toward yellow-clothed figure on highway. Prompt excerpts are abridged from the implementation, and response excerpts and numerical values are taken from the corresponding execution logs. Only relevant fields are shown, long identifiers are omitted where unnecessary, and numerical values are rounded for readability. These excerpts illustrate the interfaces rather than constitute complete executable requests. Visual inputs are described in the prompt excerpts and omitted from this presentation; camera states and rendered observations are produced by the search and execution modules. Interpreter: from input to grounded intent The input is the following instruction. The scene is an existing Blender scene; the Interpreter receives its object inventory rather than the scene file as text. USER INSTRUCTION One continuous ten-second shot. Center the yellow-clothed figures upper body with the entire rounded hairstyle visible and the road divider receding on the left. Dolly forward while zooming out to hold the figures apparent size as the roadway opens in perspective. Keep the divider clear of the torso and let its changing angle reveal depth. Ease the approach and zoom together, holding the final balanced portrait for one second. Relevant observations identify hero_01 as the yellow-clothed figure, median as the road divider, and freeway_deck as the roadway. For example, the measured bounding-box centers are (2.1826, 4.2000, 2.2473), (0, 55, 0.54), and (0, 55, 0.169), respectively. The request specifies one continuous shot lasting 10 seconds. The Interpreter receives the following role instructions together with this scene inventory and x: SYSTEM EXCERPT You are the Interpreter. Ground the scene and schedule shots, but do not construct camera plans. With shot_count=1 all requested actions belong to ONE continuous shot; do not split it. instruction describes cinematic intent; opening_intent describes the initial visual composition, not an exact camera pose. Do not output operations, camera coordinates, focal lengths, paths, cut commands, shot IDs, start/end times or source time edits. The following fields of the validated response instantiate and B. sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Extension to video-driven generation For V2V, is reference video. Reference analysis extracts camera-motion and framing cues, which the Interpreter grounds in the target scene. The resulting script is augmented with reference evidence for the relevant agents. The Scout uses reference imagery to guide opening composition, with LingBot-derived relative poses providing auxiliary motion context. The Director retains access to timestamped reference frames, reference analysis, and relative-pose evidence throughout planning and refinement. Because the reconstructed translation has unverified metric scale, these poses provide motion cues rather than target-scene camera coordinates. The motion Critic directly compares timestamped reference and rendered frames, assessing operation, direction, amplitude, timing, and endpoint fidelity, together with motion smoothness; it does not receive LingBot poses. Both settings share the atomic-operation representation and executor, with the selected opening fixed during motion-plan refinement, while using task-specific evaluation criteria. A.2 ATOMIC CAMERA OPERATIONS AND PARAMETERS Table 6 lists the 22 operations and their configurable parameters. Values are codebook defaults, which the Director may override when constructing plan. Each operation also specifies its start and end times in seconds. Angles use degrees, focal lengths use millimeters, and explicit distances use scene world units. Dolly scales are endpoint-to-initial distance ratios; Truck and Pedestal scales multiply the scene-derived subject scale. Common defaults are easing=smoothstep and, where exposed, transition_sec=0.5 and smoothing_sec=0. Operations marked additionally require target and accept an anchor, defaulting to center, except Height Follow, Aim Follow, and Frame Subject, which default to face. Both focus operations use aperture_fstop=4.0 by default. Table 6: Atomic operations, their effects, and operation-specific parameters. Common parameters are given above. No operation-specific parameters. Definitions of and The operator extracts typed relative change from an operations absolute track ˆci(t) and its reference state at tref , which is the operation start or the applicable composition boundary. Translational offsets use vector differences, angular offsets use signed angle differences about their declared axes with full turns retained, and positive scale quantities use ratios: pi = ˆpi(t) ˆpi(tref ), αi = ˆαi(t) ˆαi(tref ), rγ,i = ˆγi(t) ˆγi(tref ) . (12) Here γ denotes radial distance, orbit radius, focal length, or focus depth, as applicable. Orbit combines horizontal angular offset with radius ratio; it is not represented as simple additive position offset. The operator applies compatible relative changes to the reference or tracking-derived camera state. Translation offsets add, compatible angular offsets add within their prescribed axes, and positive scale ratios multiply. Orbit and Dolly transforms precede additive Truck and Pedestal offsets; aim composition applies base aim, Pan, Tilt, and then roll when constructing the orientation. Zoom ratios multiply the focal-length base, and explicitly enabled focus-offset ratios multiply the focus base. These are channel-specific composition rules, rather than elementwise addition of complete camera states. A.3 HYPERPARAMETERS AND COMPUTATIONAL COST All agents use gpt-6-astra with medium reasoning effort. The Scout evaluates up to six rendered candidates per round for at most two rounds. The Director allows three additional Criticguided refinement rounds and up to two validation-driven repairs per planning invocation. The opening-view and motion acceptance thresholds are set to 0.70 and 0.62, respectively. The motion Critic observes at most 10 rendered frames per evaluation in T2V and at most 16 reference plus 16 rendered frames in V2V; the opening Critic observes one rendered image per candidate. FilmFlow requires approximately 2.23 minutes and 69.5k tokens per task on average, comprising 65.9k input and 3.7k output tokens across 6.23 model calls. These averages include unsuccessful attempts and cover scene grounding, view selection, motion planning, and validation, excluding final video export.

sections.title: B CINEMABENCH
sections.content: B.1 DATASET COMPOSITION CinemaBench. CinemaBench contains 150 Blender scenes built from self-created and licensed assets, including 73 dynamic scenes with animated subjects and 77 static scenes. The scenes span diverse indoor and outdoor environments with single or multiple subjects, providing varied spatial layouts, occlusion patterns, and subject motion for camera planning. Source attribution and license information for all assets will be included in the release. Text-driven tasks (T2V). Each scene is paired with five natural-language camera instructions, yielding 750 tasks. Each T2V task consists of target scene and an instruction; the target scene supplies the subjects, geometry, and animation on which the generated trajectory is executed. Per scene, the five instructions comprise one easy, two medium, and two hard tasks. Easy tasks involve single subject and single movement; medium tasks combine two or more movements or subjects; hard tasks require coordinated concurrent operations, attention shifts across multiple subjects, or precise temporal constraints. The remaining 700 were generated with The authors manually wrote 50 instructions. gpt-6-astra, prompted with the human-written examples and conditioned on scene geometry, available objects, and existing animation. Each generated instruction passes programmatic checks, which verify that referenced objects exist, that timing is consistent with the shot duration, and that the difficulty label holds. It then undergoes model-based review for consistency with scene evidence. Instructions that failed either stage were regenerated until they passed. Reference-video tasks (V2V). subset of 60 scenes is additionally paired with 60 reference clips. Each V2V task consists of target scene and reference clip whose camera behavior serves as the generation condition. The clips are drawn from excerpts of publicly released films and selfrecorded footage, and last 10 seconds on average. Reference and generated videos may differ in scene appearance; evaluation concerns the reference camera behavior and its realization in the target scene. Split. We split CinemaBench by scene into 50 development scenes (250 T2V and 20 V2V tasks) and 100 test scenes (500 T2V and 40 V2V tasks), with no scene shared across the two splits. Development scenes are used only to build the ICL example bank (Sec. 3.3); all reported results use the test split. Table 7 summarizes the statistics per split. Table 7: CinemaBench statistics. Dev Test Total Scenes (dynamic / static) T2V tasks (easy / medium / hard) V2V tasks Human-written instructions 27 / 23 50 / 100 / 100 20 20 46 / 54 100 / 200 / 200 40 73 / 77 150 / 300 / 300 60 50 B.2 LANGUAGE OF CAMERA MOTION CinemaBench instructions describe camera behavior along four aspects: subjects, motion, framing, and temporal structure. Subject descriptions specify what the camera should observe and the spatial references around which it moves. Motion descriptions specify actions such as approaching, retreating, orbiting, rising, panning, or following, together with their direction and extent where needed. Framing descriptions specify subject placement, scale, visibility, or change of attention. Temporal expressions distinguish sequential from concurrent actions. Orbit the subject, then move closer specifies an ordered transition, whereas orbit the subject while moving closer requires rotation around the subject and radial approach at the same time. Instructions may also specify partial overlap, such as beginning push-in before an orbit ends. valid trajectory must realize both the constituent actions and their temporal organization. This is the capability tested by the Sequential-only ablation (Sec. 4.2).

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Instructions also express visual intent beyond named motions. Requests to reveal subject, shift attention, or hold close-up describe the desired visual outcome without prescribing unique operation sequence. Several combinations of atomic operations can therefore satisfy the same instruction. CinemaBench accordingly specifies no ground-truth operation sequence or trajectory for T2V; fulfillment is judged from the executed camera behavior and the rendered composition. B.3 BASELINE IMPLEMENTATION All baselines receive the same inputs as FilmFlow. None is initialized from FilmFlows outputs. GenDoP and LAMP produce trajectories in their own relative coordinate frames; we anchor frame 0 to the full pose and focal length of the scene camera at the tasks start frame, rotate the native frame-0 camera basis to match its orientation, and apply subsequent relative displacements under the same rotation, preserving roll. Trajectory scale is derived from the tasks target objects: we average the largest world-space bounding-box edge of each target at the start frame, clamped below at 0.3, to obtain subject scale s; GenDoP trajectories are scaled so that their longest axis spans 2s, and LAMP trajectories by s/64, where 64 is LAMPs native coordinate unit. Native focal lengths, when provided, are converted assuming 36 mm sensor; otherwise the scene cameras lens is used. CinemaTraj plans its own opening camera from the scene, as in its original design. For V2V, LingBot-Map and VGGT-Ω serve as direct pose-transfer baselines: their estimated camera trajectories are converted from native axis conventions to Blenders and applied in the target scene without scene-aware placement, VLM-based motion planning, or closed-loop refinement. The zeroshot VLM baseline uses gpt-6-astra with the same reference frames as FilmFlow, directly outputs camera keyframes, and interpolates between them to the full shot. GenDoP and LAMP do not track moving subjects, which reflects limitation of these methods rather than of the adaptation.

sections.title: C ADDITIONAL QUALITATIVE RESULTS
sections.content: Figures 7 and 8 provide additional comparisons for text-directed and video reference-directed camera generation. The examples complement those in the main paper with different scenes and cameramotion requirements. Within each example, all methods receive the same target scene and conditioning input. The sampled frames illustrate the progression of camera motion, subject framing, and composition, while the corresponding supplementary videos provide the complete temporal context. CASE STUDY: SCOUT REFINEMENT Figure 9 compares the opening specified directly by the Director (w/o Scout) with the Scout-selected opening for an instruction requesting loose upper-body portrait that glides forward at fixed focal length. The Director-specified 41.88 mm opening crops the top of the hair and shows little of the chest; since the focal length is fixed, the forward glide can only tighten this framing further. The Scout instead selects higher viewpoint pitched slightly downward (elevation 7.70) with shorter 26.49 mm lens, revealing the complete hair silhouette, head, and more of the chest, and leaving room for the requested push-in. This illustrates why the opening is selected before motion planning: once fixed, poor initial state constrains every subsequent operation. CASE STUDY: DIRECTOR REFINEMENT Figure 10 examines operation-plan refinement after opening-view selection. The initial and revised plans share the same instruction, target scene, and fixed opening. Frames are displayed at corresponding timestamps, and the associated operation timelines show the active intervals of the constituent motions. The Critic feedback links the observed execution problem to specific operations. The before-andafter timelines identify changes to operation selection, parameters, or temporal intervals. Displaying the rendered frames together with these changes allows the revision to be assessed in terms of both its visual effect and its underlying operation composition. The accompanying videos provide the temporal evidence needed to inspect motion continuity between the sampled frames.

APPLICATION: GREY MODEL REFERENCE AS VIDEO-GENERATION

sections.title: CONDITIONS
sections.content: Beyond executable trajectories, FilmFlows grey model renders can serve as structural conditions for video generation. Because render encodes camera motion, scene layout, and subject animation without surface appearance, one camera plan can be reused across visual styles by varying only the text prompt. Figures 12 and 13 show two renders, each paired with four videos generated by Seedance (Seedance et al., 2026). In the first example, the camera gives successive close-ups to figures in group; in the second, it leads two walking subjects while other characters enter from the right. Across stylized humans, animals, robots, and fantasy creatures, the generated videos preserve the planned framing, subject placement, and timing, while their appearance follows the prompt. This decoupling suggests that FilmFlow can act as camera planner for downstream generative filmmaking.

sections.content: Figure 12: Grey model render as video-generation condition (group close-ups). The top row shows the grey model render of FilmFlow trajectory that gives successive close-ups to figures in group. Each subsequent row is generated from the same render with different text prompt. Camera motion, framing, and subject placement follow the render, while appearance follows the prompt. Figure 13: Grey model render as video-generation condition (leading shot). The top row shows the grey model render of FilmFlow trajectory that leads two walking subjects while other characters enter from the right. The four generated videos keep the framing of the pair and the timing of the entering characters across different styles.
